prompt.context:
Our client is a cardboard manufacturer that has two plants for which we gathered the following data:

Plant A — Sales: $45,000k; Cost of Paper: 65%; Other Goods: 6%; Labor: 18%; Other Manufacturing: 6%; Depreciation: 3%; Profit: 2%

Plant B — Sales: $75,000k; Cost of Paper: 63%; Other Goods: 5%; Labor: 13%; Other Manufacturing: 5%; Depreciation: 3%; Profit: 11%
prompt.question: What does this data tell you? You have been hired to improve the performance of Plant A to similar levels as Plant B. What do you suggest?

clarifying_info.q: What industry are these plants in?
clarifying_info.a: Manufacturing of cardboard boxes for packaging.

Both plants are in Benelux, owned and operated by a central HQ division. Each plant has completely delegated authority and is its own profit centre. Each plant manages its own sales and its own customers.

clarifying_info.q: Are the production processes similar between the two plants?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Both plants have similar processes: Print, Cut, Fold, Glue. The last step (Glue) is optional and is only needed for premium customers.
Yes. Both plants have similar equipment.

clarifying_info.q: What are the salary levels at each plant?
clarifying_info.a: The average salary in each plant is the same — $45,000. Assume that everyone gets paid this amount.

clarifying_info.q: What is the workforce breakdown at Plant A?
clarifying_info.a: In Plant A: 15% of the total workforce is in sales; 35% of the workforce is represented by full time employees (management, maintenance); 50% of the workforce is represented by operators. Morale in Plant A is very low.

clarifying_info.q: What do we know about Plant B's workforce?
clarifying_info.a: All we know about Plant B is that they have 35 sales people.

clarifying_info.q: Is the customer mix different between the two plants?
clarifying_info.a: Each plant has a different customer mix, but it is not important for the case.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any issues with production runs or scheduling?
clarifying_info.a: Plant A's customers are not very good at forecasting demand and as a result the average production run at A is much less than at B. Changing production runs is a very labor-intensive step. If we could bring the number of product changes at A in line with B, we could cut operators by 10% and full time staff by 20%.

framework: Identify the profit gap: Plant A is at 2% profit vs. Plant B at 11% — the key driver is the labor cost differential (18% vs. 13% of sales).
Quantify the required labor savings: closing the gap from 18% to 13% of Plant A's $45M sales = ~$2.25M reduction needed.
Analyze the sales force: compare sales productivity per rep between plants; identify if Plant A is overstaffed in sales.
Analyze operators: investigate why operator headcount is high — link to production run frequency and demand forecasting issues.
Analyze full-time/management staff: assess whether management overhead is inflated relative to Plant B.
Assess morale: low morale may be causing productivity losses (absenteeism, errors, overtime) that inflate labor cost.
Recommend targeted headcount and process changes to recover ~$2M+ in labor savings.

questions.prompt: Calculate the total labor bill for Plant A and determine total headcount.
questions.guidance: Total labor = 18% of $45M = $8.1M (approximate to $9M is acceptable). At $45,000/person, headcount ≈ 200 people.

questions.prompt: How many sales people does Plant A have, and how does their productivity compare to Plant B?
questions.guidance: 15% of 200 = 30 sales people. Plant B has 35 sales people selling $75M → $2.14M/rep. If Plant A's 30 reps matched that, Plant A would only need ~22 reps (≈ 20). Laying off 10 reps saves ~$450K.

math.setup: Plant A sales staff = 15% × 200; Plant B productivity = $75M ÷ 35; Required Plant A reps = $45M ÷ ($75M ÷ 35)
steps: Plant A at same productivity: $45M ÷ $2.14M ≈ 21 reps (round to 20)

questions.prompt: If production run frequency at Plant A is brought in line with Plant B, how many staff can be reduced and what is the saving?
questions.guidance: Operators = 50% × 200 = 100; 10% cut = 10 operators. Full-time staff = 35% × 200 = 70; 20% cut = 14 staff. Total reduction = 24 people, saving ≈ $1.08M (≈ $1M).

math.setup: Operator reduction = 200 × 50% × 10%; FT staff reduction = 200 × 35% × 20%; Total savings = total reduction × $45,000

questions.prompt: What is the potential saving from improving morale in Plant A?
questions.guidance: Low morale can cause absenteeism and lower productivity among shift operators. Assume a 10% improvement in shift operator productivity/cost. Shift operator labor ≈ 50% of total labor bill ≈ $4.5M; 10% of that = $450,000.

math.setup: Operator labor = 50% × $9M; morale improvement saving = 10% × operator labor

questions.prompt: Sum up total identified savings. Does this close the profit gap?
questions.guidance: Sales force optimization ($450K) + production run alignment ($1M) + morale improvement ($450K) ≈ $1.9M–$2M. The target was ~$2.25M. The candidate has identified the majority of the required savings and should note remaining gap is small.

math.answer: ~$2M identified out of ~$2.25M needed — majority of the gap closed

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond labor, what other levers might help improve Plant A's profitability?

categories.name: Paper cost reduction
ideas: Renegotiate paper supplier contracts using Plant B's volume as leverage
Consolidate paper purchasing across both plants for bulk discounts
Switch to alternative paper grades for non-premium products

categories.name: Other goods cost
ideas: Standardize materials purchasing across both plants

categories.name: Revenue/mix improvement
ideas: Shift customer mix toward premium (Glue step) customers who likely pay higher margins
Improve demand forecasting with customers to increase run length and revenue predictability

categories.name: Operational efficiency
ideas: Share best practices between Plant A and Plant B management
Invest in forecasting tools or EDI with customers to reduce changeover frequency
Cross-train operators to reduce idle time during short runs

categories.name: Morale and culture
ideas: Introduce performance-based incentives tied to plant profitability
Communicate restructuring plan transparently to reduce uncertainty
Benchmark Plant A against Plant B targets to create healthy competition

recommendation: Improve Plant A's profit margin from 2% to approximately 11% by targeting ~$2M in labor savings through three levers: (1) right-size the sales force by reducing 10 excess reps, saving ~$450K; (2) bring production run frequency in line with Plant B through better customer demand forecasting, cutting 24 staff and saving ~$1M; (3) address low morale to recover ~$450K in shift operator productivity.
The combined savings of ~$2M represent the majority of the ~$2.25M labor-cost reduction needed to close the profit gap with Plant B.
risks: Workforce reductions may further damage morale if not managed carefully — require a structured change management plan.
Customers resistant to providing better demand forecasts may not cooperate; may need contractual incentives or penalties.
Remaining ~$250K gap may require additional measures such as paper cost renegotiation or revenue mix improvement.
next_steps: Develop a detailed workforce transition plan with HR to manage the 24 planned reductions.
Engage top Plant A customers on demand forecasting improvement; consider offering pricing incentives for longer production runs.
Benchmark Plant A's paper purchasing costs against Plant B and explore joint procurement.
Set Plant A a 12-month KPI dashboard tracking labor %, profit %, and morale scores.
